newsitem.title: USA: Pilots seek raise as Continental earnings climb.
newsitem.headline: Pilots seek raise as Continental earnings climb.

text.p: Continental Airlines said Tuesday it earned a record $319 million in 1996, but the good news was tempered by word that its pilots would seek a hefty pay increase.

The airline, which continues a remarkable comeback from two bouts with bankruptcy, said its healthy finances enabled it to distribute $97 million in incentive pay to employees and still end the year with a $1 billion cash balance, the highest in the company's 62-year history.
"Continental is finally in solid financial health," said Chief Financial Officer Larry Kellner.
The airline earned a record $47 million, or 61 cents a share, in the fourth quarter, which far exceeded analysts' expectations of 53 cents.
The year profit of $319 million, or $4.11 a share, topped the previous best of $224 million, or $3.15 a share, recorded in 1995.

The company said revenues jumped to $6.36 billion for the year, up from $5.83 billion a year ago. It said improved service had enabled it to win back the high-ticket business travelers who were lost when Continental was struggling through financial and labour problems earlier in the decade.

But the airline's new affluence was noted by the pilots union, which said Tuesday it wanted salaries brought back in line with the rest of the industry when negotiations for a new contract get underway in April.

"It is time for Continental management to make good with the Continental pilots. We are going to hold their feet to the fire on that issue," Capt. Bill Borrelli, vice president of the Independent Association of Continental Pilots (IACP), told reporters.
Borrelli said some of the union's 4,900 pilots are paid as much as 35 percent less than their peers at rival airlines because of concessions offered when the carrier came close to collapse.

Continental filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy first in 1983 and again in 1990. It did not emerge from bankruptcy the second time until April 1993 when Air Partners, an investment group led by David Bonderman, sank $55 million into the company.
Borrelli refused to say exactly how much the IACP would demand, but said pilots want the wage gap closed quickly.

"They (management) took it when they needed it, and they took it immediately. The company has made a remarkable and dramatic turnaround, the pilots clearly shared in part of that success, and it is time for management to belly up to the bar," he said.

But his tough talk was accompanied by words of conciliation on both sides. Borrelli complimented Continental management as the best in the industry and said pilots had "no intention" of hurting the carrier.
Continental Chairman Gordon Bethune told reporters he was confident the two sides could come to an agreement amicably.
"Pilots deserve what's fair for the pilots ... I see no reason to have acrimony, disruption and heartburn," he said.

Borrelli said the pilots' union would be open to discussing profit-sharing schemes and taking an equity stake in the airline as part of contract negotiations, but he insisted that the principal issue would be pay.
Bethune did not say what management would offer.
Continental has more than 2,000 jet and Continental Express departures daily to 132 domestic and 58 international destinations.
Its class A stock fell 87.5 cents to $28.25 on the New York Stock Exchange.
